[Slide-deck of the data story](presentation.qmd)

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(janitor)
library(ggplot2)
library(giscoR)
library(sf)
library(ggrepel)

# 1. Load and prepare GREIX data
greix_data <- read_excel(
  "data/City_Metrics_rents_sales-Mietpreis-Transaktionspreisindex.xlsx"
)

# 2. Load E8 data
e8_agg <- read_excel(
  "data/E8_topic_E__Housing_situation.xlsx",
  sheet = "housing_form_aggregated_all",
  skip = 3
)

# 3. Create DE context
de_context_wide <- e8_agg |>
  filter(FG == "all_students", FGI == "all", I == "accom_aggregated") |>
  select(indicator_item = II, DE) |>
  mutate(country_iso2 = "DE", DE = as.numeric(DE)) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = indicator_item,
    values_from = DE,
    names_prefix = "de_share_"
  ) |>
  rename(
    de_share_parents = de_share_1,
    de_share_student_accom = de_share_2,
    de_share_partner_children = de_share_3,
    de_share_other_persons = de_share_4,
    de_share_alone = de_share_5
  )

# 4. Merge
merged_data <- greix_data |>
  mutate(country_iso2 = "DE") |>
  left_join(de_context_wide, by = "country_iso2")

# 5. Create continuous time variable
plot_data <- merged_data |>
  mutate(Time = Year + (Quarter - 1) / 4)

```

1. Introduction
Our central question: How is the student housing affordability gap changing across German university cities?

Students searching for accommodation compete within the wider private rental market. Because the same student budget does not provide the same housing options everywhere, this report investigates the differences in asking rents across selected German university cities using GREIX rental market data. We examine whether previously affordable cities are experiencing faster rental growth and how this exposes students to structural vulnerabilities.

2. Analysis
To answer our central question, we break the analysis down into five specific sub-questions, using different visualisations to build the story. 

3.1. Q1: How affordable are German university cities currently?
This first chart establishes the baseline by comparing the average rent index in the most recent year across all cities.

```{r}
#| label: fig-q1
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Current Affordability Gap: Average Rent Index by City."

latest_year <- max(plot_data$Year, na.rm = TRUE)

bar_data <- plot_data |>
  filter(Year == latest_year) |>
  group_by(City) |>
  summarize(Avg_Rent_Index = mean(Rent_Index, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(Avg_Rent_Index)

ggplot(
  bar_data,
  aes(
    x = reorder(City, Avg_Rent_Index),
    y = Avg_Rent_Index,
    fill = Avg_Rent_Index
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "City", y = "Average Rent Index", fill = "Index") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```


As seen in @fig-q1, cities like Berlin, Leipzig, and Potsdam currently command the highest rent indices, while cities like Erfurt and Dresden remain relatively affordable.

3.2. Q2: Which cities are experiencing the fastest rental growth?
We then look at the change in rent over time to see where housing pressure is intensifying most rapidly.

```{r}
#| label: fig-q2
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Rental Growth: Absolute change in Rent Index over time."

growth_data <- plot_data |>
  group_by(City) |>
  summarize(
    start_rent = mean(
      Rent_Index[
        Year == min(
          Year, na.rm = TRUE)], 
          na.rm = TRUE),
    end_rent = mean(Rent_Index[Year == max(Year, na.rm = TRUE)], na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  mutate(rent_change = end_rent - start_rent) |>
  arrange(rent_change)

ggplot(
  growth_data,
  aes(x = reorder(City, rent_change), y = rent_change, fill = rent_change)
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", direction = -1) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "City", y = "Change in Rent Index", fill = "Increase") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

@fig-q2 reveals that cities like Berlin, Leipzig, and Potsdam are not only the most expensive but also experienced the fastest absolute growth. This suggests that previously "cheaper" alternatives are rapidly catching up, leaving students with fewer affordable options.

### 3.2.5. Q2.5: The Spatial Distribution of Affordability
To make the affordability gap geographically intuitive, we map the current rent index and rent growth across German university cities.

```{r}
#| label: fig-q2-5
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Spatial Map: Rent Index and Growth by City."

# 1. Get Germany map outline
germany_map <- gisco_get_countries(country = "Germany", resolution = "3")

# 2. Create a reference table for the cities in your dataset
city_coords <- tribble(
  ~City, ~lon, ~lat,
  "Berlin", 13.4050, 52.5200,
  "Bonn", 7.0982, 50.7374,
  "Dortmund", 7.4653, 51.5136,
  "Dresden", 13.7373, 51.0504,
  "Düsseldorf", 6.7735, 51.2277,
  "Erfurt", 11.0299, 50.9848,
  "Frankfurt am Main", 8.6821, 50.1109,
  "Hamburg", 9.9937, 53.5511,
  "Karlsruhe", 8.4037, 49.0069,
  "Köln", 6.9603, 50.9375,
  "Leipzig", 12.3731, 51.3397,
  "Lübeck", 10.6866, 53.8655,
  "München", 11.5820, 48.1351,
  "Münster", 7.6261, 51.9607,
  "Potsdam", 13.0645, 52.3906,
  "Stuttgart", 9.1829, 48.7758,
  "Wiesbaden", 8.2473, 50.0782
)

# 3. Join coordinates with the latest rent data
map_data <- bar_data |>
  inner_join(city_coords, by = "City") |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)

# 4. Plot the map
ggplot() +
  # Base map of Germany
  geom_sf(
    data = germany_map,
    fill = "#E8F4EA",
    color = "#A5C9A5",
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  # City markers (size based on current rent index)
  geom_sf(
    data = map_data,
    aes(size = Avg_Rent_Index),
    color = "#D32F2F",
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  # Add city labels (using ggrepel to avoid overlapping)
  geom_text_repel(
    data = map_data,
    aes(label = City, geometry = geometry),
    stat = "sf_coordinates",
    size = 3,
    min.segment.length = 0,
    box.padding = 0.5
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 8), name = "Rent Index") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

```

The map reveals that the highest rents (largest markers) are concentrated in major metropolitan areas like Berlin, Munich, and Frankfurt, while eastern cities like Leipzig and Dresden show smaller markers, visually confirming the spatial inequality of student housing affordability.

3.3. Q3: How does inflation impact the real rental burden?
High rents are exacerbated by general inflation. This chart compares nominal rent increases with inflation-adjusted (real) rents.

```{r}
#| label: fig-q3
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Inflation Impact: Nominal vs. Inflation-Adjusted Rent Index."

inflation_trend <- plot_data |>
  group_by(Time, Inflation_adjusted) |>
  summarize(
    Avg_Rent_Index = mean(Rent_Index, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Type = ifelse(
      Inflation_adjusted == 1,
      "Inflation Adjusted (Real)",
      "Nominal"
    )
  )

ggplot(
  inflation_trend,
  aes(
    x = Time,
    y = Avg_Rent_Index,
    color = Type,
    linetype = Type
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Nominal" = "firebrick",
      "Inflation Adjusted (Real)" = "steelblue"
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Rent Index",
    color = "Metric",
    linetype = "Metric"
  )

```

As @fig-q3 demonstrates, the real cost of housing is outpacing general inflation, meaning students' purchasing power is being eroded significantly.

3.4. Q4: How exposed are students to the private rental market?
To understand who is affected by these rent hikes, we analyze the E8 dataset to see where German students actually live.

```{r}
#| label: fig-q4
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Student Housing Exposure in Germany (National E8 Data)."

e8_plot_data <- de_context_wide |>
  select(-country_iso2) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Housing_Type", values_to = "Percentage") |>
  mutate(
    Housing_Type = case_when(
      Housing_Type == "de_share_parents" ~ "With Parents",
      Housing_Type == "de_share_student_accom" ~ "Student Accommodation",
      Housing_Type == "de_share_partner_children" ~ "With Partner/Children",
      Housing_Type == "de_share_other_persons" ~ "With Others (Friends, etc.)",
      Housing_Type == "de_share_alone" ~ "Living Alone"
    )
  )

ggplot(e8_plot_data, aes(x = "Germany", y = Percentage, fill = Housing_Type)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.4) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "", y = "Percentage of Students (%)", fill = "Housing Type") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

```

@fig-q4 highlights a critical vulnerability: only a small fraction of students (around 13%) are protected by student accommodation. The vast majority are forced into the private rental market.

3.5. Q5: Which student demographics are most vulnerable?
Finally, we break down housing arrangements by age group to see how vulnerability changes as students progress through their studies.

```{r}
#| label: fig-q5
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Housing Vulnerability by Age Group."

e8_age_data <- e8_agg |>
  filter(FG == "e_age", I == "accom_aggregated") |>
  select(Age_Group = FGI, Indicator = II, DE) |>
  mutate(DE = as.numeric(DE)) |>
  filter(Indicator %in% c("1", "2", "5")) |>
  mutate(
    Housing = case_when(
      Indicator == "1" ~ "With Parents",
      Indicator == "2" ~ "With Partner/Spouse",
      Indicator == "5" ~ "Living Alone"
    )
  )

ggplot(e8_age_data, aes(x = Age_Group, y = DE, fill = Housing)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Age Group", y = "Percentage (%)", fill = "Living Arrangement") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

```

@fig-q5 shows that while younger students (<22) often live with parents, students aged 22-29 are overwhelmingly pushed into the private market (living alone or with partners). These older students are hit hardest by soaring rents.

4. Discussion

The Widening Affordability Gap
Our analysis reveals a compounding crisis in German student housing. While cities like Berlin already command the highest rent indices (@fig-q1), the fastest rental growth is occurring in cities that students have historically relied upon for affordability (@fig-q2).

Crucially, our inflation-adjusted analysis (@fig-q3) shows that the real cost of renting is outpacing general inflation, meaning students' purchasing power is being eroded significantly. The visual storytelling of the E8 dataset uncovers why this is devastating: only around 13% of students are protected by student accommodation (@fig-q4). Furthermore, as students grow older, they are pushed out of parental homes and into the exposed private market (@fig-q5).

5. Conclusion
The student housing affordability gap in Germany is not just a matter of high prices; it is a structural issue. As university cities become increasingly gentrified, students are left highly exposed to private market fluctuations with very little institutional housing to shield them. Policy interventions must address both the absolute lack of student housing and the rapid inflation of the private rental market.

6. Data Source {.appendix}
GREIX rental market data (City Metrics).

Eurostudent E8 Topic E: Housing situation.

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Merge the current rent data and the growth data
quadrant_data <- growth_data |>
  left_join(bar_data, by = "City")

# Create the Quadrant Plot
p_quadrant <- ggplot(quadrant_data, aes(x = Avg_Rent_Index, y = rent_change)) +
  geom_point(color = "#D32F2F", size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = City), vjust = -0.8, size = 3, check_overlap = TRUE) +
  # Add crosshairs at the average values to create quadrants
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(quadrant_data$Avg_Rent_Index), linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(quadrant_data$rent_change), linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "The Affordability Gap: Rent Level vs. Rent Growth",
    subtitle = "Top-Right: Expensive & Rising Fast | Bottom-Left: Affordable & Stable",
    x = "Current Average Rent Index",
    y = "Absolute Rent Growth Over Time"
  )

print(p_quadrant)

```
